title: My family
seoTitle: Turkmen possessive endings and family words
intro: This unit adds **my**, **your**, **his** and **her**, which Turkmen says with endings on the noun: *kaka* (father) → *kakam* (my father). With *bar* and *ýok* they also give the way to say **I have** and **I don't have**. Two sound changes come with them: some words drop a vowel (*ogul* → *oglum*), and *k*, *p*, *ç* soften as in [A1 unit 8](a1-u08) (*kitabym*). Along the way you meet the family: Turkmen has its own word for each aunt and uncle.

sections.title: My, your, his: the possessive endings

blocks.text: Turkmen says **my house** with an ending on the noun: *öý* → *öýüm*. There is one ending for each person, and each has a form after a consonant and a shorter one after a vowel. The pronoun *meniň* (my) or *seniň* (your) can stand in front, but the ending already says whose it is, so it is often left out: *Meniň adym Aýna* and *Adym Aýna* both mean **My name is Aýna**. You met that phrase in [A1 unit 1](a1-u01); [A1 unit 10](a1-u10) explains *meniň* and *seniň*.

Three things to notice in the table. **Rounding**: after *o*, *ö*, *u* or *ü* in the first syllable, the vowel of the second syllable is *u* or *ü*, as in [A1 unit 3](a1-u03): *dostum*, *öýüm*; but a vowel that ends the word stays *y* or *i*: *dosty*, *öýi*. **The s** of *-sy* only comes after a vowel: *kakasy*, but *dosty*. **e → ä**: a final *e* becomes *ä* before *-m*, *-ň*, *-myz* and *-ňyz*: *ejäm*, *ejäň*; but not before *-si*: *ejesi*. Some writers keep the *e* (*ejem*); this course writes *ejäm* and accepts both.

items.en: This is Merdan. His father is a teacher.

blocks.text: **The family.** Turkmen splits brothers and sisters by age, and aunts and uncles by side of the family. These are the everyday words:

blocks.text: *dogan* covers any brother or sister and is the word to use when age doesn't matter: *Meniň iki doganym bar*, I have two brothers or sisters. A sister can also be called *gyz dogan*. *aga* is also used for your father's brothers and other older men on your father's side, and, after a name, for any older man you respect: *Myrat aga* ([A1 unit 3](a1-u03)). *ene* is also a poetic word for **mother**, as in *ene dili*, mother tongue.

blocks.title: Family words for everyone
blocks.text: Turkmen uses family words well beyond the family. An older woman can be called *daýza* or *eje*, an older man *aga*, and a younger person *jigim*, my little brother or sister.

sections.title: I have: a possessed noun with bar

blocks.text: Turkmen has no verb for **to have**. To say you have something, say that your thing exists: put the possessive ending on it and add *bar*. *Meniň doganym bar*, I have a brother or sister, is literally **my sibling exists**. **I don't have** uses *ýok*: *Meniň maşynym ýok*, I don't have a car.

blocks.title: *dogan* + *bar*: I have a brother or sister…

rows.en: I have a brother or sister
you have a brother or sister

you have a brother or sister (plural or polite)
they have a brother or sister

blocks.text: Ask with *barmy?* and answer with *bar* or *ýok*: *Jigiň barmy? — Hawa, bar.* After a number the noun stays singular, as after *köp* in [A1 unit 5](a1-u05): *iki doganym*, not *iki doganlarym*. [A1 unit 11](a1-u11) has the numbers in full.

items.en: Do you have a younger brother or sister? — Yes, I do.

blocks.title: Mende pul ýok or Meniň pulum ýok
blocks.text: *Mende … bar* ([A1 unit 5](a1-u05)) is about what you have **on you** right now: *Mende pul ýok*, I have no money on me. A possessive with *bar* is about what you have in your life: *Meniň pulum ýok*, I have no money. For family, it is always the possessive: *Meniň agam bar*.

blocks.title: ýok, not däl
blocks.text: Not having something is *ýok*: *Meniň wagtym ýok*, I have no time. *däl* says what something **is not**: *Bu meniň kitabym däl*, this isn't my book.

A small group of words lose the vowel of their last syllable when an ending that starts with a vowel is added. Several are words for the family and the body. Before an ending that starts with a consonant they stay whole: *ogullar* (sons), *burunda* (in the nose).

items.en: What have you got in your mouth?

blocks.text: The vowel of the ending still follows the rounding rule: *oglum* and *burnum* have *u* because their first syllable has *o* or *u*.

blocks.title: Only these words
blocks.text: Most words keep every letter: *gözüm*, *elim*, *dostum*, *doganym*. Learn the ones that drop a vowel as you meet them: *oglum*, *burnum*, *agzym*, *boýnum*. *ogulum* and *agyzym* are wrong.

sections.title: kitabym, adym: voicing with the possessives

blocks.text: The possessive endings that start with a vowel soften a final *k*, *p* or *ç* exactly as the accusative did in [A1 unit 8](a1-u08): *kitap* → *kitabym*, *aýak* → *aýagym*, *agaç* → *agajy*. Words that end in a vowel take the short endings (*-m*, *-ň*, *-sy*), and they have no final consonant to soften: *kakam*, *uýaň*.

items.en: My hair is black, my eyes are blue.

blocks.title: Adyň näme?
blocks.text: Now you can see what *Adyň näme?* from [A1 unit 1](a1-u01) is made of: *at* (name) with a long vowel, softened before *-yň* (your): *adyň*. **My horse**, with the short vowel, stays *atym*.

summary: **My, your, his**: *-(Y)m, -(Y)ň, -(s)Y*; **our, your, their**: *-(Y)mYz, -(Y)ňYz, -(s)Y* (or *-lArY*). *meniň*, *seniň* in front are optional.
After *o, ö, u, ü* the second-syllable vowel rounds (*dostum*, *öýüm*), but a final vowel doesn't (*dosty*). A final *e* becomes *ä* before *-m* and *-ň*: *ejäm*, but *ejesi*.
**I have**: possessive + *bar*: *Meniň iki doganym bar*. **I don't have**: + *ýok*. After a number, the singular.
*aga, uýa, jigi*: older brother, older sister, younger sibling; *daýy, daýza*: the mother's brother and sister; *bibi*: the father's sister; *ata, ene*: grandparents.
*ogul, burun, agyz, boýun* drop a vowel before a vowel ending: *oglum, burnum, agzym, boýnum*.
*k, p, ç* soften before the possessive: *kitabym, aýagym, çöregim*. *at* (name) → *adym*, but *at* (horse) → *atym*.
